title: Linux, kernels, and distributions
objective: By the end of this lesson you can say precisely what "Linux" refers to, why there are hundreds of versions of it, and how to pick one without agonising.

blocks.text: People use the word Linux for two different things, and the confusion causes real trouble later. Strictly, Linux is only the kernel — the core we met in the last lesson. Everything else you think of as Linux is packaged around it by someone else.
A distribution is a kernel plus decisions

A distribution (a distro) is somebody's opinionated bundle: the Linux kernel, plus the command-line tools, plus a way to install software, plus defaults about security and updates. Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Rocky, Alpine and Arch all ship the same kernel family. They differ in the decisions wrapped around it.

rows: You want the biggest pool of documentation and answers
The organisation wants vendor support and long support windows
You want the smallest possible container image
You want the newest software and will accept maintenance work

blocks.title: Which one should you learn?
blocks.text: Learn Ubuntu first. Not for technical reasons. When you paste an error message into a search box at 1am, Ubuntu answers exist. Once the concepts are yours, moving to another distro is mostly learning a different package command.
Why Linux ended up running the internet

Linux did not win servers by being friendlier. It won because the whole machine can be driven as text, which means it can be scripted, versioned and repeated. A Linux server can be installed, configured, updated, and inspected entirely through text — which means it can be automated, version-controlled, and reproduced exactly.

items: It costs nothing per machine, so running a thousand is not a licensing negotiation
It can be stripped down to almost nothing, which is why containers are Linux
Everything is text, so everything can be scripted and reviewed
The source is open, so problems can be inspected rather than guessed at

blocks.title: The security consequence
blocks.text: Because Linux runs most servers, most server-side attacks are Linux attacks. When you read an incident report about a compromised web server, you are reading about the system you are learning right now.
Versions and why the number matters

Distros ship on a schedule and support each release for a fixed period. Ubuntu labels some releases LTS — long-term support — meaning security updates keep coming for years. Running a release past its support date means the security fixes stop arriving, silently. Nothing breaks on the day it happens. The machine keeps running; the security fixes just stop arriving.

blocks.title: Find out what a machine is running
steps: Open a terminal on any Linux machine you have access to (the next lesson sets one up if you have none)
Look for the NAME and VERSION_ID lines
blocks.expected: A few lines of key=value text naming the distribution and its version. This is the first thing to check when someone asks whether a server is still supported.

cheatsheet: Linux strictly means the kernel; a distro is the kernel plus somebody's decisions
Debian/Ubuntu use apt · RHEL family uses dnf · Alpine uses apk
Learn Ubuntu first — the search results exist
Linux runs servers because it can be fully operated as text, and so automated
LTS releases get security updates for years; past end-of-support they stop silently
cat /etc/os-release tells you what a machine is actually running

choices.A: A brand owned by a single company
choices.C: The kernel — the core that manages hardware and enforces access
choices.D: A complete operating system including its desktop and applications

checkpoint.explanation: Linux is the kernel. The complete systems people install are distributions, which bundle the kernel with tools, defaults, and a package manager.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is running a distribution past its end-of-support date risky?

choices.B: The machine stops booting on that date
choices.C: Security updates stop arriving, and nothing visibly changes to warn you

checkpoint.explanation: Nothing dramatic happens on the day. The system keeps working while quietly accumulating unpatched vulnerabilities — which is precisely why it gets missed.

checkpoint.prompt: Which command shows which distribution and version a machine is running?
checkpoint.explanation: /etc/os-release is the standard file for this. whoami shows the current user and df shows disk usage — useful, but not this.
